questions: Did the unsteadiness begin suddenly, over minutes to hours?
Has it been rapidly worsening over the past few days?
Have you had a new severe headache or neck pain?
Have you developed weakness or numbness on one side of your body?
Have you had trouble speaking, understanding speech, swallowing, or controlling your facial movements?
Have you experienced double vision or difficulty coordinating your eye movements?
Do you feel as though the room is spinning?
Have you had repeated vomiting with the unsteadiness?
Have you fainted, become confused, or had a seizure?
Does your balance become much worse when you close your eyes or stand in darkness?
Do you have numbness or tingling in both feet?
Do you have difficulty knowing where your feet are without looking at them?
Have you noticed clumsiness or shaking when reaching with your hands?
Is your speech slurred or unusually slow?
Do you have new hearing loss, ringing in the ears, or ear pressure?
Do you have leg weakness or difficulty climbing stairs?
Have you had new difficulty controlling your bladder or bowels?
Have you recently had a fever, infection, or diarrhea?
Have you recently hit your head or injured your neck?
Have you recently consumed unusually large amounts of alcohol?
Have you used recreational drugs or been exposed to toxic chemicals?
Have you started or increased any medication recently, including a sedative, antiseizure drug, lithium, or chemotherapy?
Do you have diabetes, thyroid disease, vitamin B12 deficiency, or another nutritional deficiency?
Do you have multiple sclerosis, cancer, or an autoimmune disease?
Does anyone in your family have a similar balance problem or an inherited neurological disorder?
Have you had previous episodes of unsteadiness that later resolved?
Has this problem been present since childhood or early adulthood?

results: 2. Urgent non-contrast CT scan of the head
3. CT angiography of the head and neck
4. MRI of the brain with diffusion-weighted and susceptibility-sensitive sequences
brain MRI: cerebellar atrophy at one year; serial imaging over five years shows progressive ISOLATED cerebellar atrophy with no supratentorial abnormality
5. Full neurological examination, including assessment for nystagmus, dysarthria, limb coordination, truncal ataxia, and gait
Romberg test: negative - swaying is not worse with the eyes closed
deep tendon reflexes and plantar responses: normal
coordination examination (limb and truncal): limb and truncal ataxia
posture and pull test: impaired postural stability and positive pull test
8. Complete blood count, electrolytes, renal function, calcium, magnesium, liver function, and coagulation studies
serum electrolytes, urea and creatinine: normal
serum calcium, magnesium and phosphate: normal
dx_raw:
DIAGNOSIS: Sporadic adult-onset cerebellar ataxia (SAOA), a primary degenerative cerebellar disorder of unknown etiology

ALTERNATIVE: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 6 (SCA6) or another genetically mediated pure cerebellar ataxia

ALTERNATIVE: RFC1-associated late-onset ataxia (CANVAS-spectrum disease)

ALTERNATIVE: Immune-mediated or paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration
